value: One of the few grapes allowed for the late harvest Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles wines, besides its dry and off dry wines.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules for Alsace (published BO-Agri 17/10/2019), section on labelling: the mentions vendanges tardives and sélection de grains nobles must be completed by one of Gewurztraminer, Muscat, Muscat Ottonel, Pinot gris, Riesling. Wine Folly: Vendanges Tardives and SGN are made only from the four noble grapes Riesling, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Gewürztraminer. Wine Folly: single variety Gewürztraminer often made off dry. Wine Society: dry versions typical, sweeter dessert styles exist.

value: In Alsace it is full bodied and dense, with less freshness than the region's other whites and a rich, spicy palate.
source_notes: Vins d'Alsace (CIVA): full bodied, dense structure, freshness more discreet than in other Vins d'Alsace. Wine Society: full, spicy flavour.

value: Unlike the sweet Muscats of southern France, in Alsace it is nearly always made dry, with a crisp texture that keeps the fresh grape aroma.
source_notes: Vins d'Alsace: vinified dry, limpid fresh texture, differs from sweet southern French Muscat through dryness, evokes fragrance of grapes. Wine Society: nearly always bone dry in Alsace, unlike sweet wines further south. Wine Folly: Muscat made dry in Alsace.

value: In Alsace it is light bodied and supple, and is often rounded out by Auxerrois in the blend.
source_notes: Vins d'Alsace: light bodied, elegant and supple; often blended with Auxerrois for its round, generous character. Wine Society: refreshing white often blended with Auxerrois, which adds roundness.

value: One of the few grapes allowed for the late harvest Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles wines, as well as its dry and off dry wines.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules for Alsace (published BO-Agri 17/10/2019), section on labelling: the mentions vendanges tardives and sélection de grains nobles must be completed by one of Gewurztraminer, Muscat, Muscat Ottonel, Pinot gris, Riesling. Wine Folly: Vendanges Tardives and SGN are made only from the four noble grapes Riesling, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Gewürztraminer. Wine Folly: single variety Pinot Gris often made off dry. Wine Society: also makes late harvest and botrytis wines.

value: In Alsace it makes full, rich and fleshy wines, often with a smoky note, that can age for many years.
source_notes: Vins d'Alsace: ample, fleshy, full bodied, can reveal typically smoky notes. Wine Society: full, rich wines, often extremely long lived.

value: Traditionally pale and light in Alsace, it is made today in styles from rosé and light reds to fuller, deeper reds.
source_notes: Wine Society: traditionally a pale, almost rosé coloured wine, leading producers now make deeper, tannic reds. Vins d'Alsace: three Pinot Noir styles, rosé, light red, and full bodied red.

value: Most Alsace Riesling is dry, and it is one of the few grapes allowed for the late harvest Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles wines.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules for Alsace (published BO-Agri 17/10/2019), section on labelling: the mentions vendanges tardives and sélection de grains nobles must be completed by one of Gewurztraminer, Muscat, Muscat Ottonel, Pinot gris, Riesling. Wine Folly: Vendanges Tardives and SGN are made only from the four noble grapes Riesling, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Gewürztraminer. Wine Folly: Riesling made in a dry style in Alsace. Wine Society: here it is invariably dry.

value: In Alsace it is almost always dry and fuller in body than German Riesling, with a long, straight line of acidity.
source_notes: Vins d'Alsace: dry wine, very linear, noticeable weight mid palate. Wine Society: invariably dry and fuller in body with more rounded acidity (than Germany). Wine Folly: dry.

value: Sylvaner
source_notes: INAO appellation rules for Alsace list the label name Sylvaner for sylvaner B. Vins d'Alsace uses Sylvaner d'Alsace.

value: Made mostly as a light dry white, and Zotzenberg is the only Alsace Grand Cru where it is allowed.
source_notes: Wine Folly: among the Grand Crus, Zotzenberg is the only one authorised to produce Sylvaner. Vins d'Alsace Grands Crus page (seen via search excerpt): four varieties usually allowed, Sylvaner allowed in Zotzenberg. Decanter: INAO ruled Sylvaner can join the grand cru grapes, only for Zotzenberg (article text seen via search excerpt). Light: Vins d'Alsace Sylvaner page.

value: In Alsace it is a light, refreshing dry white built on lively acidity, with only discreet fruit.
source_notes: Vins d'Alsace: refreshing, light bodied, discreet fruitiness, framed around vivid acidity. Wine Society: at its most basic a lively, refreshing white with good acidity.

value: The principal grape of red and rosé Beaujolais, from Beaujolais Nouveau to the ten crus, with other grapes allowed only as a small share of mixed plantings.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules for Beaujolais (BO 15/09/2022): reds and rosés, principal grape gamay N; most accessory grapes only in mixed plantings, at most 15 percent per plot. Inter Beaujolais: gamay noir à jus blanc is the emblematic grape of the reds, also used for rosés. Wine Folly: Gamay is the main variety; lists the ten crus.

value: In Beaujolais it is mostly fruity and supple with little tannin, while crus on the granite and schist of the north, such as Morgon and Moulin à Vent, give firmer wines that can age.
source_notes: Inter Beaujolais: fruity, supple wines. Wine Society: carbonic maceration gives fruity flavours without tannin; good Morgon ages up to ten years, Moulin à Vent keeps well. Wine Folly: crus in the granite and schist north; Moulin à Vent most tannic and full bodied, Morgon to age 5 to 10 years. Decanter (search excerpt): Moulin à Vent sturdiest and most tannic of the crus.

value: The grape of white Burgundy, behind the great whites of Chablis, the Côte de Beaune, the Côte Chalonnaise and the Mâconnais.
source_notes: BIVB: Chardonnay is responsible for the reputation of the great white wines of the Côte de Beaune, Côte Chalonnaise, Mâconnais and Chablis. Wine Folly: Chablis all Chardonnay; Chardonnay critical in Côte de Beaune; Chalonnaise and Mâconnais Chardonnay.

value: The grape of red Burgundy, it dominates the Côte de Nuits and is also grown in the Côte de Beaune and the Côte Chalonnaise.
source_notes: BIVB: Pinot Noir established the reputation of the region's great red wines; Côte de Beaune about two thirds red Pinot Noir (search excerpt). Wine Folly: 80 percent of Côte de Nuits wines are Pinot Noir; Côte Chalonnaise Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

value: The leading grape of the Côte des Blancs, and the usual grape of Blanc de Blancs.
source_notes: Comité Champagne: Chardonnay is the star grape of the Côte des Blancs. Wine Folly: Côte des Blancs is mostly Chardonnay; Blanc de Blancs is usually almost entirely Chardonnay.

value: One of the three main Champagne grapes, grown mostly in the Vallée de la Marne, where it suits the clay soils and its later budding spares it from spring frost.
source_notes: Comité Champagne: suits clay soils such as the Marne Valley; less susceptible to frost as bud burst is later. GuildSomm: does well in the Vallée de la Marne because it is not as prone to frost. Jancis Robinson (search excerpt): buds later than the other Champagne varieties.

value: In Champagne it brings roundness and supple fruit to the blend, and its wines mature sooner than those of Pinot Noir or Chardonnay.
source_notes: Comité Champagne: adds roundness, supple fruity wines, tends to age more quickly than the other two grapes. GuildSomm: adds richness and fruit to the blend. Jancis Robinson (search excerpt): fruitier, earlier maturing relative of Pinot Noir.

value: The dominant grape of the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Bar.
source_notes: Comité Champagne: dominant grape in Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar. Wine Folly: Montagne de Reims focuses on Pinot Noir; Côte des Bar growers primarily plant Pinot Noir.

value: The most planted grape in the Jura, made as topped up whites, blended with Savagnin, and used as the base of Crémant du Jura.
source_notes: Interprofession des Vins du Jura guide: most widespread grape, alone or married with Savagnin. GuildSomm (Wink Lorch): Chardonnay most planted; topped up Chardonnay is Jura's most prevalent white; Crémant based on Chardonnay.

value: In the Jura it gives floral, often stony whites with brisk acidity, and takes on nutty notes when blended with Savagnin or aged under a veil of yeast.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: floral whites, citrus, white flowers; hazelnut or toasted almond in association with Savagnin. GuildSomm: nutty characters, stony mineral flavours, higher acidity from lower pH; some sous voile Chardonnay.

value: Grown on the warmer, stony sites, it is often blended with Poulsard and Trousseau, made as a single variety red, and used in Crémant du Jura.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: often used in blends, also as single variety, on gravelly soils, often married with Poulsard and Trousseau. GuildSomm: historically on warm sites with stony topsoil; increasingly a varietal red and used in Crémant.

value: In the Jura it leans towards forest floor notes alongside cherry and wild fruit.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: notes of sous bois (forest floor), cherry and wild fruit. GuildSomm: often more forest floor and animal aromas than fruit.

value: A native Jura grape that suits the cooler marl and clay soils, used for pale reds and for rosé Crémant du Jura.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: old native grape, likes heavy marl or clay soils; rosé Crémant at least 50 percent Poulsard, Trousseau and Pinot Noir. GuildSomm: indigenous, does well in cooler sites on grey blue marls; used for very pale reds and rosé Crémant.

value: Its thin skin gives a red so pale in the Jura that it can pass for a rosé, light in alcohol with small red berry fruit.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: thin skin gives a pastel colour that could pass for a rosé, light ruby, small red fruits. GuildSomm: very pale, alcohol stays light. Decanter (search excerpt): low pigment gives pale red to rosé colour.

value: The grape of Vin Jaune, made from Savagnin alone and aged under a veil of yeast, and also made topped up as a fresher white.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: Vin Jaune made exclusively from Savagnin; king grape for sous voile ageing; also ouillé. GuildSomm: core grape of vin jaune and sous voile wines, versatile in ouillé styles. Decanter (search excerpt): vin jaune 100 percent Savagnin.

value: Aged under a veil of yeast in the Jura it turns bone dry and powerful with high acidity and spice, while topped up wines stay lemony and mineral.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: sous voile gives powerful whites with complex aromas including spices; ouillé shows mineral notes of lemon and white flowers. GuildSomm: vin jaune bone dry with a whack of acidity; ouillé zingy acidity with citrus.

value: A late ripening grape that needs the warmer, gravelly sites, used for reds and for rosé Crémant du Jura.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: late and demanding grape needing lighter, gravelly, warm soils; part of rosé Crémant. GuildSomm: planted on the warmest sites with gravelly or stony topsoil; used in reds, blends and rosé Crémant.

value: In the Jura it has more colour, depth and structure than Poulsard, and the reds can age.
source_notes: Interprofession guide: rich and tannic. GuildSomm: gives rosé Crémant a darker pink colour and more vinous character. Decanter (search excerpt): more depth and structure; structured wines that can age.

value: One of the three principal grapes, with Mondeuse and Pinot Noir, for red and rosé Vin de Savoie.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules for Vin de Savoie (BO-Agri 06/07/2023): reds and rosés, principal grapes gamay N, mondeuse N, pinot N. GuildSomm: one of the three most planted red varieties with Mondeuse and Pinot Noir.

value: The most planted grape in Savoie, and the principal grape of the Abymes, Apremont and Chignin whites, at least 80 percent of plantings there under the appellation rules.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules: jacquère B principal grape for Abymes, Apremont, Chignin and others, at least 80 percent of the estate's plantings. Wine Folly and GuildSomm: the most planted grape in Savoie; GuildSomm names Apremont, Abymes and Chignin as key crus.

value: In Savoie it makes light, low alcohol, lively dry whites meant to be drunk young.
source_notes: Wine Folly: early drinking, low alcohol, lively dry wines. Decanter, Andrew Jefford (search excerpt only, article not fetchable): always light in alcohol, rarely above 11.5 percent. GuildSomm: relatively neutral wines (calls them medium bodied).

value: One of the three principal grapes, with Gamay and Mondeuse, for red and rosé Vin de Savoie, and also allowed in Crémant de Savoie.
source_notes: INAO appellation rules: principal grapes for reds and rosés are gamay N, mondeuse N, pinot N; pinot noir N a principal black grape for Crémant. GuildSomm: one of the three most planted reds, a secondary red variety.

value: In Savoie it makes structured, firmly tannic reds with lively acidity that reward a few years of ageing.
source_notes: Wine Folly: well structured acidity, integrated tannins, great ageing potential. GuildSomm: tannic on release, best between its second and eighth year. Decanter (search excerpt): more intense, structured and ageworthy than the Gamay or Pinot Noir reds.

value: In Savoie it is fuller bodied than Jacquère, and Roussette de Savoie develops honeyed, nutty notes after a few years in bottle.
source_notes: Wine Folly: Roussette should be set aside at least three years; with age develops honey, toast, nuts. GuildSomm: fuller bodied than Jacquère with admirable acidity; almond and honey notes. Fuller body rests on GuildSomm alone; ageing on Wine Folly, honey on both.

value: The most planted red grape across Bordeaux, and the lead grape of the Right Bank, above all in Pomerol, Saint Émilion and Fronsac, where it suits the cooler clay soils.
source_notes: bordeaux.com: dominant red grape of Bordeaux, grown everywhere, especially Saint Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac, on clay limestone and gravel. Wine Folly Bordeaux guide: planted across Bordeaux, main variety on the Right Bank, especially Pomerol and Saint Émilion; ripens earlier so suits cooler clay.

value: Here it gives the blend its smooth, velvety texture and full, rounded body, softening the firmer Cabernets.
source_notes: bordeaux.com: juicy, generous, velvet soft, supple rounded texture; Cabernet Sauvignon adds the structure Merlot's softness lacks. Wine Folly Bordeaux guide: smooth tannins, full body.

value: On the warm gravels of the Left Bank it ripens late into firm, upright tannins with good acidity and moderate alcohol, often with a mint or herbaceous note beside the dark fruit.
source_notes: bordeaux.com: late ripening, thrives on warm gravel of the Left Bank; cassis, liquorice, mint; vigorous firm tannins, upright structure; moderate alcohol from late ripening. Wine Folly Bordeaux guide: needs gravel to ripen; high tannin and acid, herbaceous notes.

value: Here it is lighter in colour than Cabernet Sauvignon and brings freshness, floral notes and fine tannins to the Merlot led blends of the Right Bank, above all in Saint Émilion.
source_notes: bordeaux.com: less intensely coloured than Cabernet Sauvignon; raspberry and violet; freshness, finesse, silky tannins; stronghold Saint Émilion. Wine Folly Bordeaux guide: brings tannin, acid, black fruit and floral aromas to a Merlot blend; structure in Saint Émilion.

value: Here it leans more to citrus and floral notes than to grassy ones, with a fine mineral edge, and blended with Semillon or aged in barrel it gains volume and depth.
source_notes: bordeaux.com: bright acidity, delicate mineral edge, citrus and boxwood; Semillon adds volume and texture; barrel ageing gives a deeper expression. Wine Folly: white Bordeaux is more citrus and floral than grassy and herbal; Semillon gives a richer, oilier feel.

value: On the cooler soils here it gives deeply coloured, supple reds with fleshy red fruit such as strawberry and raspberry.
source_notes: Interprofession (IVBD): on cool soils brings much colour, suppleness, fleshy red fruit; strawberry, raspberry, black cherry. INAO Bergerac product sheet: merlot evokes strawberry, raspberry and cherry.

value: Here it gives the blend its structure, with a leafy side of blackcurrant bud and green pepper beside the fruit.
source_notes: Interprofession (IVBD): brings structure and backbone; blackcurrant bud, boxwood, cassis, cedar. INAO Bergerac product sheet: cabernet evokes cassis and green pepper (poivron).

value: Here it makes powerful, fruity reds with a spicy edge, and it shows most in Pécharmant.
source_notes: Interprofession (IVBD): original, powerful and fruity grape found notably in Pécharmant; liquorice, blond tobacco. INAO Bergerac product sheet: malbec evokes spices.

value: Here it leans to blackcurrant bud and boxwood, with grapefruit, rather than tropical fruit alone.
source_notes: Interprofession (IVBD): intense aromas of blackcurrant bud or boxwood. INAO Bergerac product sheet: sauvignon evokes boxwood, grapefruit and passion fruit. INAO Côtes de Duras sheet: boxwood and blackcurrant bud in dry whites.

value: Here it takes well to noble rot, giving the sweet wines notes of ripe pear, acacia blossom, honey and hazelnut.
source_notes: Interprofession (IVBD): the great grape of moelleux and sweet wines because it lends itself to noble rot; candied lemon, acacia, honey, hazelnut, pear. INAO Bergerac product sheet: sémillon evokes ripe pear, acacia flower, hazelnut.

value: Here it brings a fresh, musky lift to the sweet wines, with orange zest beside its floral notes.
source_notes: Interprofession (IVBD): fruity and floral, intense freshness, used with Semillon in moelleux and sweet wines; honeysuckle, acacia, muscat, orange zest. INAO Bergerac product sheet: muscadelle evokes muscat.

value: Here it makes inky dark reds with firm tannins, sturdier and less plush than the Argentine style, and built for long ageing.
source_notes: INAO Cahors product sheet: only red, dark and deep colour, suited to long ageing. Wine Folly: Cahors is Malbec's most tannic form, inky dark, firm structure, versus riper, fruitier Mendoza. Hachette Vins: solid, tannic wines.

value: One of the white grapes of Irouléguy blanc, with Petit Manseng, Courbu and Petit Courbu; the appellation rules require at least two of them in every white, and it may also make up a small share of the rosé.
source_notes: Appellation rules (homologated 27 February 2024): whites from courbu, gros manseng, petit courbu, petit manseng, at least two varieties in each white; rosés may include these white grapes as accessory grapes, at most 10 percent. Hachette Vins Irouléguy page: gros manseng among the main white grapes, blended with petit manseng.

value: One of the white grapes of Irouléguy blanc, often blended with Gros Manseng and Petit Courbu; the appellation rules require at least two white grapes in every white, and it may also make up a small share of the rosé.
source_notes: Appellation rules (homologated 27 February 2024): whites from courbu, gros manseng, petit courbu, petit manseng, at least two varieties in each white; accessory in rosés, at most 10 percent. Hachette Vins Irouléguy page: petit manseng a main white grape, blended with gros manseng and petit courbu.

value: In the dry whites here it adds weight and roundness, with exotic fruit and peach, balanced by fresh acidity.
source_notes: INAO Irouléguy product sheet: whites often smell of exotic fruit and balance richness (gras) and acidity. Guide du Pays Basque (text credited to Irouléguy Distribution): petit manseng brings volume and alcohol, exotic fruit, peach and acacia. Hachette Vins: petit manseng cuvée praised for volume, roundness, balance of richness and freshness.

value: Here it is left to shrivel on the vine in the warm autumn south wind, giving sweet wines held fresh by lively acidity, fruity and floral when young and turning to dried fruit and spice with age.
source_notes: INAO Jurançon product sheet: all wines marked by liveliness; sweet wines fruity and floral when young, dried fruit and spice with age; warm dry south wind in autumn allows overripening. VinePair: sweet wines built on Petit Manseng, sugar rich grapes with a lot of natural acidity; passerillage on the vine.

value: Here it leads the dry Jurançon sec, which is lively and elegant and can keep its freshness for a few years.
source_notes: INAO Jurançon product sheet: all wines marked by liveliness; dry wines are elegant and some age a few years while keeping their freshness. VinePair: dry wines often led by Gros Manseng and sharpened by Petit Manseng's acidity.

value: Here it gives very dark, firmly structured reds with fierce tannins and high acidity, usually oak aged and needing years in bottle to soften.
source_notes: INAO Madiran product sheet: very intense colour, structured and tannic, excellent ageing ability. Wine Folly Tannat page: Madiran full throttle tannins and searing acidity, most producers use oak, cellar for a decade; Uruguay makes a more approachable style.

value: In sweet Pacherenc du Vic Bilh its grapes dry partly on the vine late into autumn, giving concentrated wines of candied fruit whose natural acidity keeps the sweetness fresh.
source_notes: INAO Pacherenc sheet: in autumn the grapes concentrate sugars and aromas for sweet whites. Appellation rules (homologated 26 November 2025): thick skinned varieties withstand overripening and passerillage. Alain Brumont (producer site, one source): late harvested, partly dried on the vine, concentrated candied fruit, natural acidity gives balance and freshness.

value: Long the workhorse grape of the Languedoc, above all in the drier west, it is now an accessory grape in the appellation rules for Languedoc reds and rosés, with a capped share.
source_notes: Languedoc appellation rules (BO 12 Dec 2019): carignan N listed under cépages accessoires for red and rosé, with a maximum proportion. Systembolaget: in Languedoc AOC reds carignan and cinsault have a capped share; carignan still dominates plantings in Corbières. The Wine Society: 'Carignan is the workhorse of Languedoc especially in the drier west.'

value: From old, low yielding vines it gives deeply coloured, concentrated and quite tannic reds with brambly fruit, while young, high yielding vines give much thinner wine.
source_notes: The Wine Society Languedoc guide: at its best, with controlled yields, Carignan makes wine that is 'deeply coloured, quite tannic, sappy with brambly fruit'. Decanter (The rise of Carignan, premium, read via search excerpt): old bush vines give tiny yields of intensely flavoured grapes; best examples come from old vines with more concentration. Decanter point is not Languedoc specific.

value: An accessory grape in the appellation rules for Languedoc reds and rosés, used above all for rosé.
source_notes: Languedoc appellation rules: cinsaut N is a cépage accessoire for red and rosé (principal only in Cabrières rosé). Systembolaget: share of carignan and cinsault capped in Languedoc AOC reds; Cabardès rosé mainly cinsault. The Wine Society: in the South of France it is widely grown and 'more often it is made into rosé'.

value: A principal grape in the appellation rules for Languedoc reds and rosés, usually blended with Syrah, Mourvèdre or Carignan.
source_notes: Languedoc appellation rules: grenache N is a cépage principal for red and rosé (with lledoner pelut, mourvèdre, syrah). Systembolaget: grenache is encouraged in Languedoc AOC reds and blended with carignan, cinsault, syrah. Wine Folly: reds have Syrah, Grenache, Carignan and Mourvèdre as major components.

value: A principal grape in the appellation rules for Languedoc whites, and with Clairette, Picpoul and Bourboulenc one of the region's most important white grapes.
source_notes: Languedoc appellation rules: grenache blanc B is a cépage principal for white. Systembolaget: grenache blanc, clairette, picpoul and bourboulenc are the most important grapes for white wines. Wine Folly: whites made mostly with Picpoul and Grenache Blanc.

value: A principal grape in the appellation rules for Languedoc reds and rosés, where it is blended with Grenache and Syrah.
source_notes: Languedoc appellation rules: mourvèdre N is a cépage principal for red and rosé, with a minimum share for mourvèdre and syrah together (figure not legible in extracted text). Systembolaget: mourvèdre and syrah now the most important grapes in Minervois; Minervois la Livinière requires grenache, syrah and mourvèdre. Wine Folly: Mourvèdre among the major red components.

value: A principal grape in the appellation rules for Languedoc reds and rosés, widely planted to replace higher yielding varieties and usually blended with Grenache or Carignan.
source_notes: Languedoc appellation rules: syrah N is a cépage principal for red and rosé. The Wine Society: 'syrah was the most obvious import and is now widely planted and is usually part of a blend with grenache and/or carignan'. Systembolaget: growers replaced high yielding aramon and alicante bouschet with syrah and mourvèdre.

value: A principal grape for Côtes de Provence reds and rosés, favoured above all for the pale rosés.
source_notes: Côtes de Provence appellation rules (BO 7 Aug 2025): cinsaut N is a cépage principal for red and rosé. The Wine Society: for pale rosé 'the light skinned cinsault often preferred over others'. Wine Folly: rosés of Coteaux d'Aix and Coteaux Varois blend Cinsault with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah.

value: A principal grape for Côtes de Provence reds and rosés and a usual part of the rosé blend; in Bandol it plays a supporting part to Mourvèdre.
source_notes: Côtes de Provence appellation rules: grenache N is a cépage principal for red and rosé. Wine Folly: Provence rosés are typically blends including Grenache; Bandol Mourvèdre is 'typically blended with Grenache and Cinsault'. The Wine Society: Bandol reds are mostly mourvèdre 'in conjuncture with grenache, cinsault'.

value: A principal grape for Côtes de Provence reds and rosés, used in blends with Grenache, Cinsault and Mourvèdre.
source_notes: Côtes de Provence appellation rules: syrah N is a cépage principal for red and rosé. Wine Folly: Coteaux d'Aix and Coteaux Varois rosés blend Grenache, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Syrah; Pierrevert reds blend Grenache and Syrah.

value: A principal grape for Côtes de Provence whites and the main grape of white Bellet; in Côtes de Provence La Londe whites it must make up at least 50 percent of the blend.
source_notes: Côtes de Provence appellation rules: vermentino B (locally called rolle) is a cépage principal for whites; La Londe whites need a minimum of 50% vermentino B in the blend. Wine Folly: 'The dominant white varietal is Rolle (Vermentino)' in Bellet. The Wine Society: 'White Bellet is mostly vermentino'. The 50% figure is from the rules only.

value: In Bandol it gives powerful, tannic reds built for long ageing, and it lends the rosés more structure than most in Provence.
source_notes: Hachette Vins (AOC Bandol): reds 'puissants et charpentés', for long keeping, tannic structure of mourvèdre softens with years; mourvèdre gives rosés more structure and longevity. Wine Folly: Mourvèdre in Bandol 'produces some of the most structured, age worthy rosés in Provence'; reds long lived. The Wine Society: mourvèdre based wines often need more time.

value: A principal grape for Côtes du Roussillon reds and an accessory one for the rosés, long the mainstay of the region's reds and usually blended with Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.
source_notes: Côtes du Roussillon appellation rules (BO 31 Mar 2022): carignan N is a cépage principal for red, accessoire for rosé. Systembolaget (Roussillon): most red is 'made mainly from carignan, increasingly joined by other grapes'; common blends are carignan, syrah, grenache and mourvèdre.

value: The leading grape of the fortified reds of Banyuls and Maury, with Banyuls Grand Cru requiring at least 75 percent Grenache, and a principal grape for Côtes du Roussillon reds and rosés.
source_notes: Gault&Millau: grenache (gris, blanc or noir) at least 50% of the Banyuls blend, 75% in grand cru. Systembolaget: fortified Banyuls and Maury are dominated by grenache; Banyuls Grand Cru needs at least 75 percent grenache. Côtes du Roussillon appellation rules: grenache N principal for red and rosé.

value: Fortified as Banyuls it gives a very sweet, full bodied red with stewed fruit and prune flavours, rich and long, that can age for many years.
source_notes: Wine Folly (Banyuls): 'Very sweet', full body, primary flavours stewed strawberry, baked prunes, dark chocolate; cellar 10+ years. Gault&Millau: best Banyuls 'bluffants de richesse, de longueur et de complexité'; old and rancio wines exist.

value: A principal grape for Côtes du Roussillon whites and, with Macabeu, one of the main grapes of the region's dry white wines.
source_notes: Côtes du Roussillon appellation rules: grenache blanc B is a cépage principal for white. Systembolaget: white production is dominated by muscat (for fortified wines), grenache blanc and maccabéo. The Wine Society: maccabeu and grenache blanc are grown mostly in Corbières and Roussillon.

value: A principal grape for Côtes du Roussillon whites and, with Grenache Blanc, one of the main grapes of the region's dry white wines.
source_notes: Côtes du Roussillon appellation rules: macabeu B is a cépage principal for white (accessory in rosé). Systembolaget: white production dominated by muscat for fortified wines, grenache blanc and maccabéo. The Wine Society: maccabeu and grenache blanc grown mostly in Corbières and Roussillon.

value: A principal grape for Côtes du Roussillon reds, where the appellation rules set a minimum share for Syrah and Mourvèdre together, and it also goes into the reds of Collioure and Maury.
source_notes: Côtes du Roussillon appellation rules (2022): mourvèdre N principal for red; mourvèdre and syrah together at least 25% (of plantings). Systembolaget: syrah and/or mourvèdre at least 20 percent (older figure, hence no number given); Collioure and Maury blends include mourvèdre. The Wine Society: Collioure reds can use mourvèdre.

value: With Muscat of Alexandria it is one of the two grapes of Muscat de Rivesaltes, a vin doux naturel that may be made from either one or a blend of both.
source_notes: INAO (appellation page, read via search excerpt, direct fetch refused): Muscat de Rivesaltes is the only vin doux naturel made from two Muscat varieties, from one alone or a blend of both. Hachette Vins: principal grapes Muscat blanc à petits grains and Muscat d'Alexandrie. Systembolaget: green muscat is a base grape of the vins doux naturels.

value: As Muscat de Rivesaltes it makes a fortified sweet wine that stays notably fresh despite its sweetness.
source_notes: Hachette Vins: 'Rond, moelleux, savoureux et frais', sweetness balanced by natural acidity. INAO (via search excerpt): very fresh wines full of finesse. INAO page read only through a search excerpt.

value: A principal grape for Côtes du Roussillon reds and rosés, where the appellation rules set a minimum share for Syrah and Mourvèdre together in the reds.
source_notes: Côtes du Roussillon appellation rules (2022): syrah N principal for red and rosé; mourvèdre and syrah together at least 25%. Systembolaget: law stipulates syrah and/or mourvèdre at least 20 percent (older figure, hence no number given).

value: In Corsica, above all in Patrimonio, it gives deeply coloured, full bodied reds with blackcurrant, blackberry and woody notes that improve with age.
source_notes: Vins de Corse interprofession: Niellucciu bright to deep red, red and black fruits, woody nuances, 'Rich, round, long, full bodied and fleshy'. Visit Corsica (regional tourism agency): reds of deep colour with blackcurrant, blackberry and woody notes, 'Tannic and full bodied, they improve with age'; king of Patrimonio.

value: It makes pale, light structured reds with a smooth, round palate, and fine rosés with red fruit and floral notes.
source_notes: Vins de Corse: light red (cherry) colour, 'Medium bodied, round and balanced'. Visit Corsica: 'a light structure and a smooth palate'; as rosé, finesse with red fruit and flowers. Rosé point from Visit Corsica only alongside interprofession's light style.

value: In Corsica it gives ample, full whites with hawthorn and white flower notes and good length.
source_notes: Vins de Corse: Vermentinu floral (white flowers, hawthorn), citrus; 'Balanced, rich, ample and powerful'. Visit Corsica: nose of hawthorn, pear, citrus and almond; 'fullness and length on the palate'.

value: As Muscat du Cap Corse it is a naturally sweet wine whose aromas move toward candied fruit.
source_notes: Visit Corsica: Muscat du Cap Corse offers naturally sweet wines with aromas of candied fruit and citrus. Vins de Corse: Muscat petits grains fruity, floral, 'on ageing, candied fruit, gingerbread'.

value: The leading grape of the southern Rhône, at the heart of the red blends of Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages and crus such as Châteauneuf du Pape, usually with Syrah and Mourvèdre. It is also made into rosé, notably in Tavel.
source_notes: Inter Rhône (vins-rhone.com): most planted Rhône grape, southern Rhône, usually combined with Syrah and Mourvèdre, red and rosé, lists Tavel, Châteauneuf du Pape, Côtes du Rhône (Villages). The Wine Society: stronghold in the south, dominates blends in Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages and the crus; Châteauneuf du Pape grenache based with syrah and mourvèdre; Tavel famed for rosé.

value: In the southern Rhône its wines are dark, earthy and densely structured, with real weight and volume on the palate.
source_notes: The Wine Society: southern Rhône grenache wines are "dark, earthy", "full bodied and often densely structured". Inter Rhône: "very fruity, round wines, with weight and volume on the palate".

value: A supporting grape of the southern Rhône, planted on its warm, well exposed hillsides and blended with Grenache and Syrah in the reds.
source_notes: Inter Rhône: widely cultivated in the southern Rhône on well exposed hillsides, long seen as an auxiliary variety, single varietal wines uncommon, blended (Grenache Mourvèdre). Wine Folly: southern grape only, adds depth to Grenache led reds with Syrah (Cairanne, Laudun).

value: The red grape of the northern Rhône crus such as Côte Rôtie, Hermitage, Crozes Hermitage and Saint Joseph. In the south it is a blending partner for Grenache.
source_notes: Inter Rhône: "In the north, Syrah reigns over reds"; Cornas Syrah only, Côte Rôtie Syrah based, Crozes Hermitage reds from Syrah; in the south Grenache blended with Syrah, Mourvèdre and others. Wine Folly: north is the birthplace of Syrah (Hermitage, Côte Rôtie, Crozes Hermitage, Saint Joseph); in the south it appears in Grenache blends.

value: Breton
source_notes: Chinon appellation rules (BO Agri 2016): came up the Loire from Nantes, "localement dénommé breton". InterLoire map: "Often referred to as Breton". Wine Folly Loire guide: local name "Breton".

value: The leading red grape of the Loire, behind the reds of Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur Champigny and Anjou Villages. It also goes into rosés such as Cabernet d'Anjou and into sparkling wines.
source_notes: InterLoire map: the Loire's first red grape, mainly used for Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint Nicolas de Bourgueil, Saumur, Saumur Champigny, Anjou and Anjou Villages; also rosés (Cabernet d'Anjou) and sparkling; Grolleau is most planted red after Cabernet Franc and Gamay. vinsdeloire.fr: ideal terroir in Chinon, Saumur Champigny, Bourgueil. Wine Folly: Chinon, Saumur Champigny, Bourgueil most famous; Anjou Villages; Cabernet d'Anjou rosé; Saumur sparkling rosé.

value: Pineau de la Loire
source_notes: InterLoire map: "CHENIN BLANC (also called Pineau de la Loire)". Wine Folly Loire guide: local names Plant d'Anjou and Pineau de la Loire. Note: neither says it appears on labels; it is a local name, labels say Chenin.

value: In the Loire it often shows quince and a fresh, mineral edge, with citrus in dry Vouvray and floral notes in the ample dry whites of Savennières.
source_notes: INAO Savennières: floral (acacia, linden) with pear, peach, quince; ample palate balanced by freshness and minerality. INAO Vouvray: dry Vouvray fresh and mineral with citrus notes. Wine Folly Loire guide: Loire Chenin baked golden apple, quince, dried flowers, crisp minerality; Savennières lime flowers, anise, grapefruit.

value: Blanc Fumé
source_notes: INAO Pouilly Fumé sheet: sauvignon blanc "appelé localement le Blanc-Fumé"; Pouilly growers say Blanc Fumé for the grape and its wines; appellation also named Blanc Fumé de Pouilly. Cellar Tours (tour operator, lower tier): Sauvignon Blanc known locally as Blanc Fumé. Applies to Pouilly only, not the whole Loire.

value: The grape behind the dry whites of the Centre Loire, in Sancerre, Pouilly Fumé, Menetou Salon, Quincy and Reuilly.
source_notes: vinsdeloire.fr: from Sancerre to Pouilly Fumé via Menetou Salon, Quincy, Reuilly and Touraine, fresh lively dry whites; Sauvignon embodies Loire dry whites. Wine Folly: Centre Loire is its home, Sancerre, Pouilly Fumé, Quincy, Reuilly, Menetou Salon; dry whites.
